title: Who Will Sit on David's Throne?
summary: King David is old and failing, and his son Adonijah, the eldest surviving prince, declares himself king with the backing of Joab and the priest Abiathar. The prophet Nathan and Bathsheba remind David of his oath that Solomon would reign, and David orders Solomon anointed at once at the Gihon spring. The city erupts in celebration, Adonijah's guests scatter, and Adonijah clings to the horns of the altar until Solomon promises to spare him if he proves worthy.
story: The story of David's house runs straight from 2 Samuel into 1 Kings. God promised David a son who would sit on his throne and build a house for the LORD's name (2 Samuel 7:12-13), but the question of which son has been hanging over the family since Amnon and Absalom died violently. Now David is too weak even to keep warm, and the succession is up for grabs. Adonijah acts first, and he has the army's commander and a senior priest behind him. Solomon, the son born to Bathsheba after the death of her first child (2 Samuel 12:24-25), has a prophet, a priest, and the royal guard. The chapter is full of human scheming, yet by its end the promise to David is moving toward fulfillment, and David himself blesses the LORD for letting him see a son on his throne.
historical:
The events are usually dated to about 970 BC, at the end of David's roughly forty-year reign and the start of Solomon's. Israel had no fixed law of succession. Neighboring kingdoms often favored the eldest son, and Adonijah, born fourth (2 Samuel 3:4) but now the eldest living, clearly assumed the throne was his. The rival parties had deep roots. Joab had commanded David's army for decades, and Abiathar had been with David since his outlaw days (1 Samuel 22:20-23). Zadok, the other chief priest, Benaiah, the commander of the royal bodyguard (the Cherethites and Pelethites, probably foreign mercenaries of Cretan and Philistine origin), and Nathan the prophet backed Solomon.

Many scholars treat 2 Samuel 9-20 and 1 Kings 1-2 as one continuous work, often called the Succession Narrative (a label made influential by the German scholar Leonhard Rost in 1926). Its question throughout is who will succeed David, and this chapter brings it to its answer. Scholars debate whether that account was written to defend Solomon's legitimacy or to expose the violence behind his rise; it reads differently depending on which emphasis one hears.
cultural:
Several customs shape the scene. Bringing a young woman to warm an aged king may also have been a test of his vigor, since a king's virility was connected with his fitness to rule; the note that he had no relations with her signals that David's strength is gone. Adonijah's chariots, horsemen, and fifty runners imitate Absalom's royal display (2 Samuel 15:1). His sacrificial feast at En-rogel, a spring just outside Jerusalem, was the equivalent of a coronation banquet: eating together sealed political loyalty.

Solomon's anointing answers each of those moves. He rides David's own mule, a public sign that the king has chosen him. He is anointed with oil from the sacred tent (the tent David had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6:17) at the Gihon spring, the city's main water source, in the valley below the city of David. The ram's horn (shofar) announces a new king, and the people shout for him. Adonijah flees to the horns of the altar, the projections at the altar's corners. Grasping them was a way of seeking sanctuary, though the law denied that protection to a deliberate murderer (Exodus 21:13-14).
literary: The chapter is a masterpiece of court drama built on repetition and timing. Nathan scripts Bathsheba's words (verses 13-14), she speaks them with additions (verses 17-21), and Nathan follows with his own version (verses 24-27), so the reader watches the same news pressed on David three times, each with small shifts that apply pressure. David's order in verses 33-35 is then repeated in its fulfillment (verses 38-40) and again in Jonathan's report to Adonijah (verses 43-48). The parallel feasts, Adonijah's at En-rogel and Solomon's procession at Gihon, run at the same time, and the sound of one reaches the other. The narrator notes pointedly that David had never once reprimanded Adonijah, echoing his failures as a father earlier in 2 Samuel.

outline.t: David's weakness and Abishag the Shunammite
Bathsheba and Nathan before the king
Adonijah's feast breaks up and he seeks sanctuary

doctrines.note: God is barely mentioned in the action, yet his promise to David is carried forward through the plans of a prophet, a mother, and a dying king. The chapter shows God working through ordinary, even messy, human choices.

Kingship in Israel was meant to rest on God's choice, not on a prince's self-promotion. Adonijah exalts himself; Solomon is anointed at the king's command with a prophet and priest present, and David credits the LORD with providing him.
The note that David never corrected Adonijah connects the crisis to years of parental neglect. The chapter shows how failures inside a household can spill into public disaster.

words.note: Mashach, to anoint by pouring oil on the head. It marked kings, priests, and sometimes prophets as set apart by God for a task. From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, Messiah. Solomon's anointing by priest and prophet marks him as the LORD's chosen, not merely his father's favorite.

Nagid, leader or ruler, a title used for someone designated by God to lead his people (Saul and David are both called nagid in 1 Samuel). David appoints Solomon nagid over Israel and Judah, stressing that he rules as God's designated servant.

Shaba, to swear an oath. The chapter turns on an oath David swore that Solomon would reign, an oath not recorded earlier in 2 Samuel. Nathan and Bathsheba appeal to it, and David reaffirms it with a new oath by the living LORD.

Qeren, horn. The horn of oil anoints Solomon, and Adonijah grasps the horns of the altar. In Hebrew idiom horn also signifies strength, so the word frames both the new king's power and the defeated rival's desperate appeal to God's protection.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ runs through the promise to David. God swore that a son of David would reign, and here, despite rivalry and intrigue, a son of David is anointed and seated on the throne. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as the son of David and the Anointed One, the Messiah, to whom God gives the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32-33). The contrast with Adonijah is also instructive: he exalted himself, while the New Testament describes Christ as the one who humbled himself and was then exalted by God (Philippians 2:8-9). And Solomon rides into Jerusalem on a royal mule with the people rejoicing, a scene some readers compare with Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey amid crowds proclaiming the son of David (Matthew 21:5-9), though the Gospels themselves cite Zechariah 9:9 rather than this passage.

hard.q: Did David really promise the throne to Solomon, or did Nathan and Bathsheba manipulate a confused old man?
hard.a: The oath they cite is not recorded anywhere earlier, and the scene is full of careful staging, so some readers suspect a palace coup dressed up as loyalty. Others point out that 2 Samuel 12:24-25 says the LORD loved Solomon and sent Nathan to give him the name Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD, which suggests Solomon was already marked out, and that 1 Chronicles 22:9-10 and 28:5 present God as choosing Solomon. They also note that David responds with full clarity and a detailed plan, not confusion. The narrator doesn't settle the question explicitly. What he does make clear is that David confirms the choice with an oath by the LORD, and that the result fulfills God's purpose even though the human methods were political.

questions: Adonijah was never corrected by his father. How does what is left unsaid in a family shape the people in it?
Adonijah exalted himself, while Solomon was appointed by another. Where do you feel the pull to promote yourself rather than wait to be given a place?
God's purposes moved forward through people with mixed motives. How does that encourage or trouble you when you look at your own church or family?
